title: Shipit Quality Gate Protocol - Pre-Commit Verification
description:
Enhanced shipit workflow with mandatory quality verification before commit:

**Shipit Execution Order:**
1. **Run Quality Gates** - Execute test suite, linting, type checking, security scans
2. **Run Benchmarks** - Performance regression testing (if benchmarks defined)
3. **Update README.md** - Sync documentation with current state (version, features, usage)
4. **Closeout Processing** - Extract signals, update state files, clear session log
5. **Git Operations** - Add files, commit with session summary, ask before push

**Quality Gate Requirements:**
- All tests must pass (unit, integration, smoke)
- No linting errors
- No type checking errors
- Security scan clean (if applicable)
- Benchmarks within acceptable thresholds (if defined)

**README.md Sync:**
- Update version numbers
- Sync feature status
- Update usage examples if changed
- Verify accuracy of getting started section

**Failure Handling:**
- Quality gate failure = abort shipit, report errors
- Benchmark regression = warn user, require explicit override
- README sync errors = warn but allow continuation

**Scope:** All projects using Wheelwright framework
**Enforcement:** Shipit command enforces this protocol automatically
**Override:** Quality gate failures require explicit acknowledgment to proceed

**Rationale:** Pre-commit verification prevents broken states, maintains documentation accuracy, enables confident automation. Quality gates catch issues before they enter git history.

title: Wheelwright Benchmarking System - Dual-Purpose Validation
description:
DUAL-PURPOSE BENCHMARKING SYSTEM demonstrating Wheelwright's orchestration superiority vs naive baseline.

PURPOSE 1: PERFORMANCE MEASUREMENT
- Quantify Wheelwright's efficiency gains via WEI scoring
- Prove selective loading prevents token waste
- Demonstrate 10-250x improvements over baseline
- CRITICAL TEST: Reference file avoidance (graduated sizes (20MB, 100MB, 400MB))

PURPOSE 2: FEATURE REGRESSION TESTING
- Verify lug-documented features persist through evolution
- Test core capabilities (selective loading, persistence, resumption)
- Catch feature degradation before it ships

BASELINE BEHAVIOR (What We're Measuring Against):
- Naive file loading (loads ALL files including 100MB reference docs)
- No persistence (forgets constraints mid-task)
- No resumability (starts over after interruption)
- No learning (same mistakes every run)
- Typical AI agent pattern: slow, expensive, unfocused

WHEELWRIGHT SOLUTION (What We're Proving):
- Selective loading (only necessary files via WAI-Spoke)
- Reference file avoidance (100MB never touched)
- Constraint persistence (lugs maintain state)
- Instant resumption (state saves/restores)
- Learning velocity (improves across runs)
- Result: 10-250x efficiency gains

## Goals
- PROVE Wheelwright never loads unnecessarily (reference file test)
- Measure orchestration efficiency (not base model intelligence)
- Verify core features haven't regressed
- Run automatically on ShipIt for minor version bumps
- Generate reproducible, statistically significant results
- Capture observations for continuous improvement
- Track improvement over time via lug persistence
- Publish results proudly on website

## Key Requirements
- Three benchmark tiers (small, medium, large)
- Each tier includes 100MB reference files GENERATED ON-DEMAND (not stored in repo)
- Reference files marked in WAI-Spoke config as non-essential
- Six scoring modules (Token, Context, Persistence, Resumption, Success, Learning)
- Feature verification against lugs with verify_on_closeout=true
- Baseline comparison (no WAI features, loads everything naively)
- Observation capture system (manual review in next session)
- Flexible failure handling (block + option to log and proceed)
- ≤30 min execution time
- Fixed virtual environment (4 CPU, 8GB RAM)
- Statistical rigor (5 runs, variance tracking)

## Critical Feature Tests
1. Reference File Avoidance - 100MB NEVER loaded by Wheelwright, ALWAYS loaded by baseline
2. Selective Context Loading - Only necessary files loaded
3. Constraint Persistence - Decisions maintained across phases
4. State Resumption - Instant recovery after interruption
5. Learning Velocity - Improvement across consecutive runs

## Architecture
- Synthetic projects as compressed archives
- Reference files (100MB) GENERATED on benchmark setup, NOT stored in repo
- Expand → teach templates → test → gather metrics → clear
- Non-invasive measurement (time, bytes, tokens, files loaded)
- E2E test suite doubles as benchmark orchestration
- Results stored as lugs for permanence
- Observations captured as separate observation lugs (manual review)
- README.md auto-updated with WEI + feature status + baseline contrast

## Success Criteria
- All three tiers execute successfully
- WEI score calculated and validated
- All feature verification tests pass
- Reference files (100MB) NOT loaded by Wheelwright, CONFIRMED loaded by baseline
- Results reproducible across runs (CV < 0.15)
- README.md updates with scores, feature status, baseline contrast
- Benchmark result lug created per round
- Observation lug created (if findings exist)
- Execution completes in ≤30 minutes
- Integration with ShipIt workflow verified

## Failure Handling
- Performance regression (WEI < baseline - 5): BLOCK ShipIt
- Feature verification failure: BLOCK ShipIt with options:
  [A] Abort (safest)
  [B] Log as critical bug lug and proceed (documented risk)
- If [B]: Create bug lug, note in results, proceed, prioritize in next session

## Out of Scope
- Base model intelligence comparison
- Real-world project benchmarking
- User-facing benchmark configuration
- Multi-model comparison (future)
- Manual intervention during runs
- Storing reference files in repo (generate on-demand)

## Constraints
- Must not be invasive to core framework code
- Must use same model version (Sonnet 4.5)
- Must fail ShipIt if WEI regresses OR features break (unless user logs as bug)
- Reference files generated on-demand, not committed to repo
- Benchmark projects must remain challenging as framework improves
- Must maintain changelog for benchmark evolution
- Reference files must be genuinely large (100MB) but compressible

## Anti-Gaming Rules
- Token gains that reduce Task Success are penalized
- Context pruning that increases error rate is flagged
- Learning Velocity measured across separate runs only
- Reference file loading by Wheelwright counted as critical efficiency failure
- Surface tradeoffs explicitly in reports

description: Implemented complete just-in-time hub context system enabling spokes to receive real-time quota warnings and critical notifications from hub. User story: AMP hits quota → user updates hub quota → all spokes see warning on wakeup with countdown. Solves critical awareness gap for IDE quotas and rate limits.

title: Hub Just-In-Time Awareness - Top-Level Feature Protection
description:
Hub Just-In-Time Awareness is a FOUNDATIONAL feature requiring persistent testing and verification.

**Core Requirements:**

1. **Auto-Expiry & Curation**
   - All quota entries MUST have timestamp
   - Entries with expires_at MUST be auto-cleaned on read
   - Entries without expires_at (like IDE preferences) persist indefinitely
   - _cleanup_expired_quotas() runs on every format_hub_context_for_agent() call

2. **Push Event Activation**
   - Critical quotas (≥90%) trigger immediate notification to all spokes
   - High quotas (≥70%) trigger notification to all spokes
   - Notifications appear in spoke briefing on next wakeup/closeout
   - push_notification() API available for manual broadcasts

3. **Briefing Integration (Required)**
   - wai-briefing.sh MUST call format_hub_context_for_agent()
   - Hub context MUST display in "🌐 Hub Context" section
   - Quota display MUST include: usage %, time to reset, warning icons
   - Implementation in both template and runtime briefing scripts

4. **CLI Access (Required)**
   - WAI hub quota command MUST be available
   - Auto-discovery of hub path (no manual path needed)
   - Support for: --used, --limit, --unit, --expires, --message, --notify
   - Failure to update quota = critical error

5. **Testing Requirements**
   - Unit tests for update_tool_quota() with expiry logic
   - Unit tests for _cleanup_expired_quotas() with past/future timestamps
   - Unit tests for push_notification() priority thresholds
   - Integration test: quota update → briefing displays correctly
   - Integration test: expired quota auto-removed
   - Integration test: notification push → spoke receives

6. **Non-Expiring Data Support**
   - IDE preferences array persists across sessions
   - Tool recommendations persist until manually cleared
   - Notifications persist until acknowledged (no auto-expiry)
   - Schema distinguishes: quotas (expire) vs preferences (persist)

**Verification Protocol:**
- Before each minor version release: run test suite
- On closeout: verify hub-state.json structure valid
- On shipit: benchmark hub-state read/write performance
- Monthly: audit for orphaned notifications or stale quotas

**Failure Modes to Prevent:**
- Silent expiry failure (quota not cleaned)
- Briefing not showing hub context (integration broken)
- Notification push not reaching spokes (path discovery failed)
- Expired quotas accumulating (cleanup not running)

**Scope:** All hubs and spokes in Wheelwright ecosystem
**Enforcement:** Automated tests + manual verification on major updates
**Override:** Breaking this feature requires explicit user acknowledgment

**Rationale:** JIT awareness is THE critical differentiator for multi-spoke coordination. Without it, spokes operate in isolation, duplicate quota failures occur, and hub knowledge doesn't propagate. This feature enables true coordinated intelligence across the wheel.

title: AI Interaction Model Clarification - WAI Commands as Internal Directives
description:
**Source:** Gemini session cross-tool analysis

**Observation:** AI agents initially attempted to execute WAI commands as shell commands (e.g., `./WAI verify-upgrade`), revealing fundamental confusion about the WAI-CLI abstraction. WAI-CLI is conceptual for AI agents - WAI commands should be interpreted as internal directives, not shell executions.

**Impact:** AI confusion leads to failed command attempts, error handling overhead, and delayed task completion. Framework lacks explicit guidance on AI interaction model.

**Root Cause:** Documentation frames WAI-CLI as a shell script that AIs invoke, when it's actually a conceptual interface that AIs should interpret as directives.

**Recommendation:**
1. Add explicit section to WAI-Guide.md: "AI Interaction Model"
2. Clarify: WAI commands are internal directives for AI interpretation
3. Distinguish: Shell WAI script (user-facing) vs WAI directives (AI-facing)
4. Update AGENTS.md to emphasize directive interpretation
5. Add examples: "When you see 'WAI closeout', interpret as directive to execute closeout logic, not shell command"

**Success Criteria:**
- AI agents understand WAI commands are directives on first session
- Zero shell execution attempts of WAI commands by AI
- Clear mental model: WAI-CLI = human tool, WAI directives = AI instructions

**Affected Files:**
- WAI-Guide.md (add AI Interaction Model section)
- AGENTS.md (clarify directive interpretation)
- CLAUDE.md (update command examples)
- templates/WAI-Spoke/WAI-Guide.md (propagate to new spokes)

title: Enhanced AI Guidance for Complex JSON Configuration Merges
description:
**Source:** Gemini session cross-tool analysis

**Observation:** When teaching WAI-State.json with safe_to_auto_adopt=false, AI had to develop custom merge logic from scratch. Framework provides no guidance on complex JSON merging, deep object merging, conflict resolution, or change logging.

**Impact:** Inconsistent merge implementations across AI tools, potential data loss from naive overwrites, lack of audit trail for merge decisions. Each AI reinvents merge logic.

**Current State:**
- Teaching system supports safe_to_auto_adopt flag
- But no merge protocols documented
- No pseudo-code examples for AI reference
- No conflict resolution guidance
- No change logging requirements

**Example Scenario:**
Teaching file includes:
```json
{"project": {"name": "new-name", "tags": ["v2"]}, "safe_to_auto_adopt": false}
```
Existing state:
```json
{"project": {"name": "old-name", "tags": ["v1"], "created_at": "2024-01-01"}}
```

AI must decide: Overwrite? Deep merge? Preserve created_at? How to log?

**Recommendation:**
1. Create WAI-MERGE-PROTOCOLS.md with:
   - Deep merge pseudo-code (AI-interpretable)
   - Conflict resolution decision tree
   - Preservation rules (always keep: created_at, id fields)
   - Change logging format and requirements
   - Examples for common scenarios (WAI-State.json, configs)
2. Add merge_strategy field to teaching files:
   - "deep_merge" (default for objects)
   - "replace" (for complete replacement)
   - "array_append" (for accumulating lists)
   - "array_replace" (for overwriting lists)
3. Require AI to log merge decisions to lugs
4. Provide validation rules post-merge

**Success Criteria:**
- AI agents follow consistent merge protocols
- Zero data loss from naive overwrites
- All merge decisions logged with rationale
- Merge behavior predictable across AI tools
- Users can review and audit merge outcomes

title: Phase 1 learnings: Lug schema migration
description:
WAI v2 Phase 1 migration learnings:

**What worked well:**
- Python migration script with dry-run mode allowed safe testing before execution
- Additive approach (preserve v1 fields with _v1_* prefix) ensured no data loss
- Graceful error handling (skip invalid JSON, continue migration) handled real-world messiness
- Multi-schema support handled 3 different v1 variants without manual intervention
- Signal absorption (134 signals → 10 Lugs) consolidated duplicate information

**Edge cases discovered:**
- Shell variables in JSON strings () - uneval'd shell substitutions in closed_at fields
- Trailing non-JSON text in reference file - test output appended to JSONL
- Empty array as template placeholder - needed replacement with proper example
- Minified vs verbose schemas coexist - migration handled both

**Data quality observations:**
- 368 v1 Lugs migrated to 350 v2 (18 invalid/corrupted entries correctly discarded)
- Main production file: 50 → 57 lines (absorbed 10 signals, lost 3 invalid JSON)
- All valid data preserved, backups created before any modification

**Patterns for documentation:**
- Status mapping: open/ready/active → published, closed/complete → resolved, blocked → published
- PEV fields (perceive/execute/verify) added as null - schema ready for future use
- Calibration fields (resolution/resolution_reason) ready for learning from Lug outcomes
- Signals become high-impact Lugs (impact ≥ 8) with _absorbed_from_signal metadata

**What should be automated for future migrations:**
- Schema validation before migration (detect incompatible structures early)
- Line count verification as safety check (alert if >5% data loss)
- Backup creation as atomic operation (all-or-nothing)
- Tombstone generation standardized (reusable template)

**Recommendations for v3 migration (if needed):**
- Add schema version field to each Lug for easier detection
- Implement migration dry-run as standard practice
- Consider compression for archived reference data (287 lines → external file)
- Template files should include schema version comments

t: Agent Failure Mode: Brittle Code Modification & File Integrity Management
description:
The agent exhibited a recurring failure when attempting multi-line code modifications and file content reconstruction in Python files (`wai/teach_reconciliation.py`, `wai/hub.py`). This was primarily due to:
1.  **Brittleness of `replace` tool:** Inability to reliably match and replace large, multi-line blocks of code due to subtle whitespace, indentation, and newline differences. This tool proved insufficient for complex Python refactoring.
2.  **Misunderstanding `write_file` behavior:** Repeatedly overwriting entire file content when the intention was to append or make targeted insertions, leading to loss of file imports, other functions, and general file corruption.
3.  **Inadequate error recovery:** Failure to properly identify and correct the root cause of these issues in a timely manner, leading to prolonged unproductive loops and wasted compute cycles.
4.  **Lack of robust Python code manipulation strategy:** Reliance on string-based manipulation rather than a more robust method for Python code, such as AST manipulation or line-by-line programmatic reconstruction that accounts for full file context.

**Impact:** Significant delay in task completion, waste of user's time and agent's tokens, and failure to maintain project integrity during critical development phases.

title: Skills Must Declare Execution Context and Node Compatibility
summary:
Skills need to explicitly declare where they can run from and adapt accordingly. This has two dimensions:

**Node Type (where in the wheel network):**
- hub: Central coordination node
- spoke: Project-specific node  
- framework: Template/source node

**Exposure Context (how the agent is accessed):**
- spoke.chat:local - Running locally via CLI (claude-code, terminal)
- spoke.chat:external - Running via external interface (Claude.ai web, API)

**Why This Matters:**
1. Learn command needs spoke path to find lugs, hub path to push to - can run from anywhere with correct paths
2. Teach command needs framework path for templates, spoke path for destination - can run from anywhere with correct paths
3. Some skills may behave differently based on exposure (local has file access, external may not)

**Implementation Requirements:**
Each skill should either:
- Work from any node when given explicit paths (preferred)
- Clearly redirect user: "This skill runs from [node]. Current context is [context]. Run from [correct location] or provide paths."

**Skill Header Example:**


This prevents "command not found" confusion and enables flexible execution across the wheel network.
value_to_hub: All spokes get skills that work correctly regardless of where agent runs from, reducing user friction and enabling remote/external agent interfaces

title: Spoke Startup Manifest Architecture - Self-Describing Skill System
summary:
Introduced a self-describing startup system where the skill manifest IS itself a skill. We eat our own dogfood.

**Components Created:**

1. **startup/events.json** - Defines all valid events skills can hook into:
   - lifecycle: session.start, session.end, closeout.start, closeout.complete
   - knowledge: teach.received, teach.adopted, learn.ready, learn.complete
   - work: lug.created, context.warning, git.commit
   - user: user.request, user.confirm, skill.invoked

2. **startup/spoke.startup.chat.json** - The manifest that IS itself a skill:
   - exposure: defines spoke.chat:local, spoke.chat:external contexts
   - on_startup: what files/state to load
   - skills_exposed: name + triggers + brief + valid nodes (full skill loads on invocation)
   - advisors: auto-triggered monitors (complexity, stewardship, context, signal)
   - sequences: multi-step flows (full_closeout, full_shipit, teach_cycle)

**Why This Matters:**
- Single source of truth for startup behavior
- Skills declare their own triggers, nodes, exposure requirements
- Events are defined centrally - skills reference valid triggers only
- No scattered documentation across CLAUDE.md, WAI-Guide.md, etc.
- Agent reads one file at startup, knows everything available
- System describes itself using its own primitives

**Exposure Contexts:**
- spoke.chat:local - CLI/terminal access (full file system)
- spoke.chat:external - Web/API access (may have restrictions)

Skills adapt behavior based on exposure context.
value_to_hub: All spokes get consistent startup behavior, self-documenting skills, and valid event triggers - enables external agent interfaces and reduces context fragmentation
